LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$

    v_status varchar(20);   -- same type as customers.status

    -- the population order deterministic (ascending total spend), matching the
    -- reference result set produced by the original procedure.
    FOR rec IN
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count
        FROM   orders o
        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name

        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';

            (customer_id, customer_name, total_spend, order_count, tier, computed_at)
        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,
             v_tier, now());
    END LOOP;

    -- The original fetched one arbitrary customer row purely as a status
    -- sanity check; LIMIT 1 reproduces that, and STRICT keeps the behavior
    -- identical should the table ever be empty.
    SELECT status INTO STRICT v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;

    COMMIT;
END;
$proc$;

            v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

-- ============================================================================
-- sp_monthly_report — migrated from Oracle PL/SQL to PostgreSQL plpgsql
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Aggregates order line items into a per-category monthly revenue report.
-- Oracle constructs replaced:
--   * table-anchored row variable        -> composite variable of the table's
--                                           row type (v_row monthly_report)
--   * constant aggregate over a one-row
--     Oracle table                       -> plain SELECT COUNT(*) (PostgreSQL
--                                           needs no FROM clause for that)
--   * null-safe aggregates               -> COALESCE
--   * user-defined "no data" exception   -> RAISE EXCEPTION tagged with the
--                                           no_data_found SQLSTATE (P0002)
--   * ROLLBACK/RAISE in exception blocks -> EXCEPTION handlers; entering a
--                                           handler already undoes the
--                                           protected block's work, and the
--                                           explicit ROLLBACK mirrors the
--                                           original whole-transaction discard
--   * end-of-procedure commit            -> COMMIT in the outer block (it must
--                                           stay outside the protected block,
--                                           because a block with an EXCEPTION
--                                           clause runs inside a subtransaction)
-- ============================================================================

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_monthly_report(p_month IN varchar)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_row      monthly_report;   -- one report row, anchored to the table
    v_has_data numeric := 0;
BEGIN
    -- The original counted a constant one-row Oracle table, which always
    -- yields 1; a bare SELECT does the same here.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_has_data;

    BEGIN
        -- Recompute this month from scratch.
        DELETE FROM monthly_report WHERE report_month = p_month;

        -- Aggregate order lines by product category.  The ORDER BY keeps the
        -- population order deterministic (revenue descending), matching the
        -- reference result set produced by the original procedure.
        FOR rec IN
            SELECT p.category                                    AS category,
                   COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue,
                   COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0)                 AS units_sold
            FROM   order_items oi
            JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
            GROUP  BY p.category
            ORDER  BY revenue DESC, category ASC
        LOOP
            v_row.report_month := p_month;
            v_row.category     := rec.category;
            v_row.revenue      := rec.revenue;
            v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

            INSERT INTO monthly_report
                (report_month, category, revenue, units_sold)
            VALUES
                (v_row.report_month, v_row.category, v_row.revenue, v_row.units_sold);
        END LOOP;

        IF v_has_data = 0 THEN
            -- Original raised a user-defined "no data" exception; tagged with
            -- the matching SQLSTATE so the named handler below catches it.
            RAISE EXCEPTION 'no data available for monthly report %', p_month
                USING ERRCODE = 'P0002';
        END IF;

    EXCEPTION
        WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
            -- Handled condition: discard the transaction and finish quietly,
            -- exactly like the original handler.
            ROLLBACK;
            RETURN;
        WHEN OTHERS THEN
            ROLLBACK;
            RAISE;   -- re-raise to the caller
    END;

    COMMIT;
END;
$proc$;

## 41\.8. Transaction Management [\#](#PLPGSQL-TRANSACTIONS)

In procedures invoked by the `CALL` command as well as in anonymous code blocks (`DO` command), it is possible to end transactions using the commands `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK`. A new transaction is started automatically after a transaction is ended using these commands, so there is no separate `START TRANSACTION` command. (Note that `BEGIN` and `END` have different meanings in PL/pgSQL.)

Here is a simple example:

```

CREATE PROCEDURE transaction_test1()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    FOR i IN 0..9 LOOP
        INSERT INTO test1 (a) VALUES (i);
        IF i % 2 = 0 THEN
            COMMIT;
        ELSE
            ROLLBACK;
        END IF;
    END LOOP;
END;
$$;

CALL transaction_test1();
```

-- ============================================================================
-- sp_customer_tier — migrated from Oracle PL/SQL to PostgreSQL plpgsql
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Computes the lifetime tier of every active customer from their orders.
-- The original read the aggregates through an explicit cursor loop and wrote
-- one summary row per customer; that structure is preserved here with a
-- plpgsql query loop.
-- Oracle constructs replaced:
--   * null-safe status check  -> COALESCE
--   * current timestamp       -> now()
--   * single arbitrary row    -> LIMIT 1 (with STRICT to keep the same
--                                empty-table failure mode)
--   * final transaction commit -> omitted: in PostgreSQL the changes become
--     permanent when the CALL statement completes, which is the same
--     observable behavior.  (Bare COMMIT inside a procedure is only legal in
--     top-level CALLs; issuing it here would fail whenever the CALL runs
--     inside an already-open transaction.)
-- ============================================================================

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_customer_tier()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    rec      record;        -- cursor loop variable
    v_tier   varchar(20);   -- tier label assigned inside the loop
    v_status varchar(20);   -- same type as customers.status
BEGIN
    -- Tiers are always recomputed from scratch.
    DELETE FROM customer_tiers;

    -- Cursor loop over the per-customer order aggregates.  The ORDER BY keeps
    -- the population order deterministic (ascending total spend), matching the
    -- reference result set produced by the original procedure.
    FOR rec IN
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count
        FROM   orders o
        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name
        ORDER  BY total_spend ASC, o.customer_id ASC
    LOOP
        IF rec.total_spend >= 1000 THEN
            v_tier := 'GOLD';
        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';
        END IF;

        INSERT INTO customer_tiers
            (customer_id, customer_name, total_spend, order_count, tier, computed_at)
        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,
             v_tier, now());
    END LOOP;

    -- The original fetched one arbitrary customer row purely as a status
    -- sanity check; LIMIT 1 reproduces that, and STRICT keeps the behavior
    -- identical should the table ever be empty.
    SELECT status INTO STRICT v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;
END;
$proc$;


-- ============================================================================
-- sp_monthly_report — migrated from Oracle PL/SQL to PostgreSQL plpgsql
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Aggregates order line items into a per-category monthly revenue report.
-- Oracle constructs replaced:
--   * table-anchored row variable        -> composite variable of the table's
--                                           row type (v_row monthly_report)
--   * constant aggregate over a one-row
--     Oracle table                       -> plain SELECT COUNT(*) (PostgreSQL
--                                           needs no FROM clause for that)
--   * null-safe aggregates               -> COALESCE
--   * user-defined "no data" exception   -> RAISE EXCEPTION tagged with the
--                                           no_data_found SQLSTATE (P0002)
--   * ROLLBACK inside the exception
--     handlers                           -> the EXCEPTION clause itself: a
--                                           block with handlers forms a
--                                           subtransaction, so by the time a
--                                           handler runs, the protected
--                                           block's changes are already
--                                           rolled back — the same outcome as
--                                           the original rollback, and it
--                                           works in every CALL context
--                                           (explicit transaction control is
--                                           only legal in top-level CALLs)
-- ============================================================================

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_monthly_report(p_month IN varchar)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    rec         record;         -- cursor loop variable
    v_row      monthly_report;  -- one report row, anchored to the table
    v_has_data numeric := 0;
BEGIN
    -- The original counted a constant one-row Oracle table, which always
    -- yields 1; a bare SELECT does the same here.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_has_data;

    -- Recompute this month from scratch.
    DELETE FROM monthly_report WHERE report_month = p_month;

    -- Aggregate order lines by product category.  The ORDER BY keeps the
    -- population order deterministic (revenue descending), matching the
    -- reference result set produced by the original procedure.
    FOR rec IN
        SELECT p.category                                    AS category,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0)                 AS units_sold
        FROM   order_items oi
        JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
        GROUP  BY p.category
        ORDER  BY revenue DESC, category ASC
    LOOP
        v_row.report_month := p_month;
        v_row.category     := rec.category;
        v_row.revenue      := rec.revenue;
        v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

        INSERT INTO monthly_report
            (report_month, category, revenue, units_sold)
        VALUES
            (v_row.report_month, v_row.category, v_row.revenue, v_row.units_sold);
    END LOOP;

    IF v_has_data = 0 THEN
        -- Original raised a user-defined "no data" exception; tagged with the
        -- matching SQLSTATE so the named handler below catches it.
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'no data available for monthly report %', p_month
            USING ERRCODE = 'P0002';
    END IF;

EXCEPTION
    WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
        -- Entering this handler has already rolled back this block's changes
        -- (the DELETE and any INSERTs), just like the original handler; the
        -- condition is handled quietly and the procedure ends.
        RETURN;
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        -- This block's changes were rolled back on the way in; propagate the
        -- original error to the caller, as the source procedure did.
        RAISE;
END;
$proc$;

| Oracle construct | PostgreSQL translation |
|---|---|
| `NVL(c.status,'ACTIVE')` | `COALESCE(c.status,'ACTIVE')` |
| `sysdate` | `now()` |
| `WHERE ROWNUM = 1` | `LIMIT 1` (+ `INTO STRICT` to keep the empty-table failure mode) |

| final `COMMIT` | omitted — the `CALL` statement's own commit gives identical semantics (bare `COMMIT` in a procedure is only legal in top-level CALLs and hard-errors otherwise) |
